title: PHP2Shell: AI Found the PHP Flaw First. Why Sites Worldwide Went Offline, and How to Check Yours
description:
On October 21, 2026, PHP issued an emergency security update for two flaws known together as PHP2Shell: the flaw is in PHP itself, and with no login, a single request can run code on the server. AI found it two months earlier, but a leak pushed the patch forward by a day, and government sites worldwide, pixiv and Wikimedia took themselves offline first. This video uses one comparison (a car recall: the defect is in the engine, not the body) to explain why it concerns you and what happened in those four days, then demonstrates on an Ubuntu test machine: seeing 8.3.6 in php -v does not mean unpatched; you have to read the package's changelog.
For anyone in Taiwan with their own website, anyone managing WordPress or an online store for a company, or anyone who saw "websites down worldwide" and wants to know what to do.

Recorded October 25, 2026. The four security releases, "only updating is the complete fix" and distributions receiving the patches in advance follow php.net's October 21 advisory; the 2024 audit, the leak and the timing of the early release follow the PHP Foundation's blog; the 70% of websites, the models used and the timeline follow Wiz's research post; the 03:02 UTC firewall follows the Cloudflare blog; the October 17 honeypot follows the AWS Security Blog; Taiwan's roughly 28,000 public-facing sites, roughly 200 government agency sites, and the order of patch, WAF, suspend follow iThome's report on the October 22 press conference by the director-general of the Administration for Cyber Security; the shutdowns by country follow the BBC; the Japanese prime minister's and the Cloudflare CEO's figures follow their original posts on X; the Japanese services that paused follow Japan Cyber Watch. The three local commands and their output were really run on 2026-10-25 on Ubuntu 24.04.5, PHP 8.3.6 (cli) and dpkg 1.22.6; the fixed package version for 24.04 follows ubuntu.com's CVE page. "My take is" and "I can't find out" are the owner's opinions. This video does not demonstrate the attack.

Commands in the video:
php -v
dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n' php8.3-cli
zcat /usr/share/doc/php8.3-cli/changelog.Debian.gz | head -n 4

On your site, who manages PHP, you or your host? What version did you find? Tell me in the comments.

chapters.seventy: Affected if I don't write PHP?

4649.text: On August 11, researcher Ryan Austin used GPT-5.6 Sol to produce an exploit, the kind from the opening: one request gets in.

9ey5.text: On October 21, PHP issued an emergency security update for two flaws known as PHP2Shell.

cdnj.text: An hour before release, Japan's prime minister posted an urgent request on X.

nc3h.text: You might ask: my site runs WordPress, I don't write PHP myself.

h7nb.text: It does: the flaw is in PHP itself.

3ppu.text: No login needed: one request can run code on your server, read passwords out of memory, or alter your site.

vwd9.text: The flaw sits that deep, so even spotless site code can't stop it.

vw9g.text: So if AI found the flaw first, why did sites worldwide still have to shut themselves down?

69ry.text: In ten minutes you'll have four things: how AI found it two months early, why the patch moved up a day;

hsxu.text: the four security versions, and one check a version number alone won't show you.

9agr.text: I said it concerns you, but how likely? Of sites whose server language can be identified, nearly 70% run PHP: WordPress, Drupal and Joomla all do.

iecr.text: That "flaw in PHP itself" line is like a car recall: the defect isn't your paint or seats, it's the engine.

x493.text: Your site's code is the body; PHP is the engine underneath.

c633.text: Even a site that only prints Hello World can be hit.

qy4i.text: Highest risk: servers running PHP as an Apache module.

byuv.text: A request arrives and the attack hits before your code even runs.

86sc.text: And Taiwan? Early tally from the digital ministry's cyber agency: about 28,000 public sites run PHP,

rsu6.text: about 200 government sites among them; as of the director's press conference, no breach reported.

gffq.text: So how long has this flaw been in PHP? Over a decade, since version 5.4 in 2012.

v5ur.text: In fact, in 2024, during PHP's first external security audit in years, a core developer already saw signs of this memory issue.

92tm.text: But no one proved it exploitable; each fix had a cost.

rayj.text: A small team needed unanimity; the fix stalled and restarted, for months.

daec.text: The PHP Foundation itself later wrote:

uyhr.text: The delay was a structural failure.

wavj.text: So who pulled it out of the drawer?

rb3w.text: On July 30, security firm Calif, under OpenAI's open-source patching program Patch the Planet, began auditing PHP;

jmju.text: The root cause was that 2024 problem.

i6qv.text: Two weeks later, Google-owned security firm Wiz used the fourth-generation Gemini, that is Argon, plus GPT-5.6 Sol, and independently found the same flaw,

sqad.text: and got it working on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

2eju.text: From the day Austin handed in the exploit, fixing it became the Foundation security team's top priority; patch set for October 22.

26df.text: Wiz says that with these models, what one researcher finished in a week used to take a whole team of top people months.

gbaz.text: Wiz compares it to the 2014 Heartbleed flaw: that one was a crypto library, this is the web language itself.

j6sz.text: It may be a similar turning point for the AI era.

m35m.text: You may wonder: is AI finding flaws really good or bad? Park that for now; see what happened over the next four days.

dy8w.text: Over two months of secrecy broke in the last two days.

df33.text: On the afternoon of October 20, a post appeared on Hacker News: two PHP remote code execution flaws were coming.

7t2j.text: The post even got the score wrong, calling it a perfect 10; PHP's own rating is 9.2.

d2mf.text: Four hours later, PHP gave early notice: the patch was moving up a day.

p4ua.text: Moved to 2 p.m. UTC on the 21st, that's 10 p.m. in Taiwan.

hafe.text: Half an hour later, co-discoverer Calif accidentally posted an attack demo video; deleted, but already out there.

4eea.text: 3 a.m. on the 21st: Cloudflare enabled firewall rules for all customers, free plans too.

pmy2.text: At 7:41, container company Chainguard released patched images over six hours early.

q6jq.text: Attackers could read the fix off them.

ubbs.text: At the promised 2 p.m., all four security versions shipped on time.

nxcc.text: How fast did attacks come? Cloudflare's CEO says ten hours before the advisory, they saw thousands of attempts;

2fht.text: 45 minutes after it, tens of thousands; two hours, hundreds of thousands; under half a day, over a million.

a87y.text: Amazon's decoy server, a honeypot, logged an attack attempt on the 17th, three days before the leak.

yqd7.text: So with no patch yet and attacks on the way, what can a site do?

wppc.text: The UK's cyber security centre was blunt:

vh8a.text: No time to patch or mitigate? Consider a shutdown.

bqis.text: Japan's cybersecurity authority also said suspending sites is an effective way to reduce risk.

m52w.text: So the night before the patch, as if a recall notice had just gone up, owners pulled over first.

s8y2.text: Even the Dutch cyber agency's own site closed;

wnky.text: 32 UK government sites and parts of Wikimedia went offline too.

vrdu.text: Remember the post from the start? At 9:55 p.m. Japan time, just an hour before the patch release,

nauj.text: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi posted an "urgent request" on X:

56c5.text: Check tonight whether your site uses PHP.

khrf.text: Taiwan ordered no shutdown. Its steps: patch first;

g97x.text: if it's too old to patch, a web firewall first; only when neither works, suspend public services.

ksrk.text: One difference from a recall: a recall can be scheduled, this couldn't; that number came in half a day.

42gu.text: The patch is out; how do you know yours is patched?

fx7j.text: The official advisory, link below: the title ends in two words, update now.

zq2u.text: The four promised versions, one per branch, are in this table: your branch's last number must match or exceed the one listed.

pacb.text: 8.1 and below get no official releases; rely on your distro or host.

53hk.text: I tried it on my test machine: the version command came back 8.3.6.

2qhy.text: Against that table, the 8.3 branch isn't fixed until the last number is 36;

m5s9.text: Mine ends in 6, which looks thirty versions behind, so I must be hit, right?

p9ke.text: Don't jump to conclusions: this machine runs Ubuntu, and PHP was installed from the distro's package.

c8xq.text: The question: which version did Ubuntu actually install?

57xv.text: Ask another way: not PHP itself, but the package manager: what version has it recorded? Command in the description.

f5zi.text: What comes back isn't just the bare three numbers; the distro's own package number follows.

cffr.text: Last step, open the package's own changelog: one command, and the first four lines are enough; also in the description.

94he.text: Line one: after the version, the security update channel;

eea5.text: Line three says security update; line four is the patch's filename, which holds PHP2Shell's two CVE numbers, the flaws' ID numbers.

ur3m.text: In fact, the patch was already in. The fixed version on Ubuntu's CVE page is exactly the string the package manager just printed.

pmmz.text: PHP's own advisory says so: Linux distros and long-term support vendors got the patch early and shipped it in old-numbered packages.

bvkf.text: Like a recall that fixed the engine: the year on the registration stays; you check the service record.

rvnm.text: On your own machine, do the same check by one of three cases.

mm34.text: Self-built or Windows: version at or above the four fixed releases;

48dz.text: Linux packages: the package version, and the CVE numbers in the changelog;

w9gx.text: Managed hosting: ask your host two things: which PHP version, and what day the patch went in; "we're on it" from support isn't an answer.

emqi.text: Three common misconceptions: updating WordPress doesn't update PHP; PHP comes from the host or the container image;

tgt8.text: Rumor: disable a session setting, you're safe; PHP says it blocks only some paths and can't replace updating;

anbx.text: A note on the 23rd still said turn that setting off; same message: mitigation, not a patch.

pcpg.text: After patching, restart PHP's worker processes; the old ones still run the old code.

dv5w.text: Okay, the question we parked: AI finding the flaw first, good or bad?

gx6w.text: My take: finding flaws got faster; fixing them didn't, it still goes through several pairs of hands.

pmgi.text: Maintainers pick a fix, distros package it, hosts deploy it,

v48u.text: and the slowest step was that two-day leak.

duf7.text: How many of Taiwan's 28,000 sites are fixed today, I can't find out; the cyber agency says it will keep tracking.

n4we.text: Three things now: today, check by those three cases; if managed, ask your host;

7hcv.text: this week, plan to move sites on 8.1 or below to 8.3 or above; 8.2 security support ends at year end too;

6k5e.text: after that, add your host's security notices where you'll see them.

eedd.text: Recall the opening question? AI found it first; so why did sites shut themselves down?

w9rt.text: Because a patch is a chain, not a file; until the chain is done, pausing first is safest.

dknd.text: On your site, who manages PHP, you or your host? What version did you find? Tell me in the comments.

c6mc.text: Subscribe: each video gives you one call you can make right away.
